speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To address Mr Leong Mun Wai's question about the actions the Ministry has taken to protect Singapore's copyright in the case of a composer plagiarising the song "Count on Me Singapore", let me set out the details of this incident.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We first received feedback that the song, "We Can Achieve", was featured in several videos, some of which were of school children, apparently from India, singing the song.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This song was almost identical to "Count on Me, Singapore", save for minor differences, such as replacing the word "Singapore" with "India", and a line in the song which goes, "we are told no dreams to hold that we can strive for".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the videos, the students appeared to be expressing their love for their country and the song was not disrespectfully treated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The publisher of the song "We Can Achieve" subsequently came forward to acknowledge that the song seemed to be substantially copied from "Count on Me, Singapore" and apologised for it, as well as removed it from their platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We did not believe that there was any ill will or malice intended and hence accepted this apology.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Shortly after, one Mr Joey Mendoza, then alleged that he, in fact, was the one who wrote the song, "We Can Achieve" in 1983.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was an untenable assertion, given that this song, as I mentioned earlier, was practically identical to "Count on Me, Singapore".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If his claim was right, it would be a direct affront to our own ownership and interest in the national song "Count on Me, Singapore".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We thus pressed Mr Mendoza to substantiate his claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If he could not, then he should withdraw them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We were prepared to initiate legal proceedings, if necessary, to protect our position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, we also undertook extensive fact-checking in Singapore and in India, to refute Mr Mendoza's claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We obtained confirmation of contemporaneous and documentary evidence of the writing of the song, "Count on Me, Singapore".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Jeremy Monteiro, a respected musician and Cultural Medallion recipient, was witness to the events at the material time, contemporaneously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members might have read his account in the news of how he worked alongside Mr Hugh Harrison when Mr Harrison composed the song in 1986.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Mendoza also wrote to us to confirm that the song "We Can Achieve" has been taken down from known networks and platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have thus let the matter rest on this basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The current legal position for our national songs and symbols includes the Singapore Arms and Flag and National Anthem legislation (SAFNA), as well as the Copyright Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The legislation around the use of the national symbols and the Government's stance on copyright of the national songs are intended to prevent misuse that might diminish or denigrate the standing of such symbols and songs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, we should not take umbrage at every such use, and resort to legal remedies each time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A careful judgement is made in each case, as to whether and if so what, action is to be taken, along the considerations which I have outlined above.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Gerald Giam's question on whether the Government regularly checks for possible infringements of our symbols, the Ministry monitors reports on the use of the national songs and symbols by the media, does online sensing and also takes public feedback.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our symbols have generally been treated with respect and dignity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There have been rare cases of flag-burning, which usually involved other forms of misconduct, and were dealt with swiftly under the appropriate regulations in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Giam may be aware that MCCY first announced in September 2020 that it had initiated a review of the rules governing the national symbols.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are also looking into whether there is a need to enhance IP protection for our symbols.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Honouring and respecting our symbols, however, is not something that is achieved only by legal regimes or protecting copyright.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We must also cultivate and sustain a strong connection and respect that Singaporeans feel for symbols and songs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of us have a part to play in upholding our symbols and passing them down to future generations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And to that end, MCCY has convened a citizens' workgroup on our national symbols to seek the public's feedback and views on this review, because these symbols indeed, belong to all of us.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our national songs were written by various composers, both local and foreign, some of whom were working for advertising agencies contracted by the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm that the Government holds the exclusive copyright to the music and lyrics for all our national songs, such that none of these composers or advertising agencies can claim ownership whether now or in the future?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The answer to Mr Giam's second question is yes, permission needs to be sought and the legal ambit and regulations that govern this will be set out in the Copyright Act, as with any other ownership of copyright.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are some other arrangements where the copyright in the composer and lyricist might be different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But in all situations, where it is either owned by the Government or managed by the Government, to that extent, permission would be sought before any third party uses or performs these songs on any other platform.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One is when MCCY put up the first statement on "Imitation is the best form of flattery", was it before Mr Mendoza came out to claim his rights?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second question is, since Mr Mendoza had come up originally to claim his rights, after we had done our check on our rights, why did we not actually press the issue further and asked him to admit plagiarism, rather than just letting him go like that?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because in Singapore, we are aspiring to be the global original arbitration centre.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Dealing with such infringement of IP rights lightly, will affect our aspirations to be that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On Mr Leong's first question, the original post by MCCY was before Mr Mendoza surfaced his claims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I explained earlier, the first video or the first series of videos were of school children in a respectful setting, using the song albeit without permission.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it was in that context that the first message that Mr Leong refers to was put up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Subsequently, when Mr Mendoza asserted his claim, as I explained in my answer earlier, Mr Mendoza's assertion was a direct challenge to our own ownership and proprietary interest in the song, then things took a different turn and we pressed Mr Mendoza to withdraw his claims, which brings me to my second point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He withdraws his position he previously took on "We Can Achieve".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to Mr Leong's point about assertion of interest in our copyright, assertion of our position and our ownership of such copyright, that was what we did precisely with Mr Mendoza.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That, I believe in this context, was a far more efficient outcome that was achieved in a matter of several days, as opposed to being caught up in protracted legal action, which could potentially take a fairly long period of time.
